objectives: Explain what a token is and why models see ids not text
Describe how embeddings map ids to vectors

slides.title: Part 1 — Why text has to become numbers
slides.body: A neural network is a pile of matrix multiplications. It cannot multiply the word **cat**. Before any model can learn anything about language, text has to be turned into numbers — and *how* you do that quietly decides what the model can and cannot represent.

slides.title: The model never sees letters
slides.body:
Type a sentence into the playground on the right and watch it shatter into colored chunks. Each chunk is a **token**, and each token is really just an integer — an index into a fixed vocabulary.

The model receives a list of integers like `[464, 2415, 7]`. It has no idea those came from the word "transformer". All linguistic structure — grammar, meaning, the fact that "cats" is the plural of "cat" — has to be *re-learned* from how those integers co-occur.

This is the first design decision in every language model, and everything downstream inherits it.

slides.title: Three ways to split text
slides.body:
There is a spectrum of choices for *what counts as a token*:

- **Characters.** Vocabulary ≈ 100 symbols. Tiny vocab, but sequences become very long and the model spends capacity re-discovering that `c-a-t` is a unit.
- **Words.** Short sequences, but the vocabulary explodes (every typo and proper noun) and you can never represent a word you didn't see in training — the **out-of-vocabulary** problem.
- **Subwords.** The modern answer: common words stay whole (`the`, `cat`), rare words split into reusable pieces (`token` + `ization`). Bounded vocab *and* nothing is ever truly unknown.

Every production LLM uses subwords. We will see exactly how they are built in the BPE lesson.

slides.title: Counting the cost: the sequence-length tax
slides.body:
Tokenization is not just correctness — it is *cost*. Transformer compute scales with the **number of tokens**, and attention scales with the *square* of it.

Take a 1,000-character paragraph. A character tokenizer emits ~1,000 tokens. A subword tokenizer emits ~250. Attention cost is roughly $O(n^2)$, so the ratio is:

$$\frac{1000^2}{250^2} = \frac{10^6}{6.25\times10^4} = 16\times$$

The character model does **16× more attention work** for the same paragraph. Tokenization choices show up directly in your GPU bill.

question.question: A word-level tokenizer is trained, then deployed. A user types a brand-new product name it never saw. What happens?
options: It is mapped to a single special "unknown" token, losing all information in that name
The tokenizer invents a new vocabulary entry on the fly
The model reads it character by character automatically
question.explanation: A pure word tokenizer has a vocabulary fixed at training time. Anything unseen collapses to a single `<unk>` token — the model literally cannot tell one unknown word from another. This out-of-vocabulary failure is the core reason subword tokenization replaced word tokenization.

question.question: Tokenizer A averages 4 characters/token; tokenizer B averages 2 characters/token. For the same document, roughly how does B's self-attention compute compare to A's?
options: About 4× more (cost grows with the square of token count)
The same — attention cost doesn't depend on the tokenizer
About half (fewer characters per token is cheaper)
question.explanation: B produces 2× as many tokens for the same text (half the characters per token). Self-attention is O(n²) in the token count, so doubling n quadruples that term: (2n)² / n² = 4×. Token efficiency is a real architectural lever, not a cosmetic detail.

slides.title: Part 3 — The subtleties that bite
slides.body: Tokenization looks trivial until it silently breaks something. Three classic traps.

slides.title: Whitespace, case, and the leading space
slides.body:
Most modern tokenizers attach the **leading space to the word**. So `"cat"` at the start of a string and `" cat"` mid-sentence are *different tokens*. This is why a model can behave differently depending on spacing, and why prompt formatting matters more than people expect.

Casing is similar: `Apple`, `apple`, and `APPLE` may be three different tokens. The model has to *learn* they are related — it is not given for free.

Try it in the playground: type `cat`, then ` cat` with a leading space, and watch the token id change.

slides.title: Numbers and code tokenize badly
slides.body:
Digit strings are a notorious weak spot. `1234` might be one token while `1235` splits as `12` + `35`. The model is handed no consistent place-value structure, which is a real source of arithmetic errors in LLMs.

Code has the opposite problem — indentation, brackets, and rare identifiers fragment into many tokens, inflating sequence length. Tokenizers tuned for code (more whitespace and symbol merges) measurably improve coding models. The tokenizer is part of the model's inductive bias, not a neutral preprocessing step.

question.question: Order these from FEWEST to MOST tokens produced for the same 500-word English paragraph.
question.explanation: Word-level emits roughly one token per word (~500). Subword splits some rare words into 2–3 pieces, so it is a bit higher (~650). Character-level emits one token per character (~2,800). Fewer tokens means shorter sequences and cheaper attention — but word-level pays for it with the out-of-vocabulary problem, which is why subword wins in practice.

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body:
- The model only ever sees **integers**; every bit of meaning is learned from how those integers co-occur.
- **Subword** tokenization is the modern standard: bounded vocabulary, no true out-of-vocabulary words.
- Token count is a **cost** lever — attention is $O(n^2)$ in tokens.
- Spacing, casing, numbers, and code all tokenize in non-obvious ways that change model behavior.

**Next:** [Word embeddings](/wiki/embeddings) — how each token id becomes a learned vector the network can compute with — then [BPE tokenization](/wiki/bpe-tokenization), the exact algorithm that builds a subword vocabulary.
